name: As the Moon Swallows the Stars

characters.name: Anthony Messina
characters.summary: Anthony Messina is a 48-year-old forensic psychiatrist in [[Lake Cranesford]] and the man the whole book is built from. He is never described by the narrator: the reader knows him only through what he produced, kept and annotated across one year — until the form breaks in Part Two.
characters.appearance: Italian-American, working build going soft, glasses for reading. The reader builds him from his work, not from description.
characters.voice: Clinical default. Lapsed-Catholic syntax surfaces under stress (examination-of-conscience) — ''However.'' standing alone. Working-class Italian specificity flickers in the notebook. Drily funny when well. Brittle and irritable late, never drained — he stays a professional.
characters.backstory:
Western PA. Penn State undergrad; OSU Wexner for med school and residency. Came home for practice.

His father is a carpenter — stable, nurturing. His mother was a military JAG investigator: forensic by training, principled and methodical. He is her son in a different forensic discipline. Both parents now live at [[Lake Arthur Retirement Village]].
characters.wants: He is still trying when she dies. That is what makes it tragedy.
characters.secrets: Has been at his edge for years and doesn’t know it. By the time the book opens he is running at 100% in his work and roughly 30% in his life, holding the imbalance by force of habit.

sections.title: Caseload
sections.text: Sex-offender risk assessments, violent-offender parole evals, post-attempt mandates, competency to stand trial, NGRI. Not custody. See [[The case docket]].

sections.title: Condition
sections.text:
Has been at the edge of his capacity for years. He doesn’t know it. He’s busy, he’s tired, he’s going to catch up next week — he’s been telling himself that for a decade. Holds work clean; life thins. The grenade reveals what was already true.

== What thins, in absence ==
* The vacation he doesn’t book (the email thread that ends without his reply)
* Calls home to his parents, monthly to nothing
* Grocery lists on the back of Theresa’s memos — early year, then gone
* Mass: the family together early; Theresa alone late
* Notebook entries: daily → weekly → monthly
* Morning runs his Apple Watch logs in April, absent by August
* Sunday brunches he attends becoming brunches he sends Theresa to alone
* Theresa’s voicemails accumulating, some unlistened

The order it goes: family first, friends second, self third, work last.

sections.title: Tics
sections.text:
* Hates the small black pen; uses it anyway
* Apple Watch heart-rate alert as silent witness
* Reaches for objects and misses when distracted
* Particular about candle scent
* The cracking leather patient chair

sections.title: Religion
sections.text: Lapsed by attrition, not rupture. Twenty years whittling. The architecture remains; the practice ended quietly without a date.

sections.title: The pocket notebook
sections.text:
The honest mode: a pocket Moleskine, three days per page, bullets, blue pen, sloppy. It degrades by thinning — daily becomes weekly becomes monthly. The voice doesn’t degrade; the frequency does. == Early (week 8, April) == 
Mon 4/6   * leave @ 2 (Greystone reservation)
          * prescription pickup
          * Reeves f/u re: school records
Tue 4/7   * breakfast w/ T — eggs
          * dictation: Cantwell
          * T's mom — 4 ribs (??)
Wed 4/8   * milk
          * G's permission slip (sign)
          * Brandt review — stable
Thu 4/9   * court — Petrak 9 AM
          * prep notes Cantwell
          * "Sopranos" w/ T
Fri 4/10  * trash out
          * Easter mass program (already?)
          * call Dad
== Late (week 43, January) == 
Mon 1/13  * Hartman — records pending
          * V. won't look at me.
Tue 1/14

Wed 1/15  * picked up cleaning
Thu 1/16  * —
Fri 1/17

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The presence the documents build. The man who tried. The man who couldn’t see the stars when the moon was too bright.

== To decide ==
* Clinical note typeface — Courier New (dictated and transcribed) or a clean sans (typed into an EHR)? See [[Style sheet]].

mar.events:
Weeks 1–4 — calibration. The March calendar spread opens the book.
* [[Marcus Reeves]] intake (Mar 8) — competent, and then: ''However.'' Marginalia dated 3/14. Report issued wk 3–4; mitigation referral.
* [[Cantwell]] SVP eval at [[SCI Mercer]] (standing case; the southbound GPS).
* [[Brandt]] conditional-release review (wk 1).
* Text to Vince: “good luck today” / “thx old man”.
* Theresa’s voicemail, listened: “Picking up V’s stuff at 5. Gas in your truck. Love you.” 0:14
* Save-the-date from [[Joey Messina|Joey]] arrives (wk 4). Sunday brunch.
mar.notes: Calendar: dense, clean, every weekday filled, planned in one sitting, clean fountain-pen hand. Grocery lists still appearing on the back of Theresa’s memos.

apr.events:
Weeks 5–8 — Easter.
* [[Petrak]] found incompetent (wk 5); sent for restoration.
* Joey and [[Annabel Coster|Annabel]] home for Easter.
* [[Sayles]] progress note (compliant).
* Theresa’s study calendar thickens.
apr.notes: Notebook still full (week 8): Greystone reservation, “call Dad”, Easter mass program. Apple Watch logs morning runs.

may.events:
Weeks 9–12 — anniversary.
* Routine session layer.
* Phone call with his parents at [[Lake Arthur Retirement Village|Lake Arthur]].
* 25th anniversary dinner at [[The Greystone]] (wk 12) — receipt, photo, notebook entry. The marriage unguardedly visible. (Scored moment.)

jun.events:
Weeks 13–17 — summer.
* [[Kessler]] opens (~wk 14) — the malingerer; cat-and-mouse begins.
* Brandt review #2 (wk 16).
* Joey’s summer call — Anthony distracted, gives the wrong advice; Joey figures it out.
* 4th of July (wk 17).

jul.events:
Weeks 18–21 — Theresa’s exam, her bad day.
* Kessler caught (wk 19) — a clean, dry win.
* Sayles progress note (~wk 18).
* Cantwell eval #2 (wk 20).
* Theresa takes the promotional exam. Her fatal-accident day (wk 20): “I’m OK.” Post-it in his lunch bag.

aug.events:
Weeks 22–26 — Eva enters.
* [[Hartman]] opens (wk 22) — capital mitigation, running underneath everything from here.
* Theresa passes the exam.
* [[Eva Miller]] intake (wk 26) — one more file in a busy drawer.
aug.notes: Calendar still dense and clean; it absorbs Eva’s standing appointment. By August the morning runs are no longer in the Watch data.

sep.events:
Weeks 27–30 — Eva builds.
* Eva’s early sessions; her middle-of-bed sleep change (wk 30).
* Petrak returns restored (~wk 30) — the case’s real turn.
* Brandt review #3 (wk 30).
* Wedding invitation arrives (wk 29).
* The vacation not booked — the travel quote sits in the drawer; Theresa’s “Should I book it?” gets no reply.

oct.events:
Weeks 31–34 — restoration certified, broken promise.
* Petrak certified (wk 34).
* [[Allbright]] opens (wk 33) — the longest notebook entries of the year run here.
* Bachelor weekend (wk 33) — he misses Friday.
* The broken promise: Gianna’s college-essay request — “tomorrow morning, promise.” The essay sits on his desk for months.
oct.notes: Calendar still planned ahead but with slight gaps. The first “?” appears, beside a Sunday brunch.

nov.events:
Weeks 35–38 — concussion, finding, ghost.
* [[Vincent Messina|Vince]]’s concussion (ER fax, wk 35).
* Cantwell eval #3 (wk 36).
* Allbright finding rendered (wk 38) — charged, personal.
* [[The ghost case]] (wk 38): death notice of a former patient. He clips it. Writes nothing.
* Thanksgiving.

dec.events:
Weeks 39–42 — Vince home, the date, Christmas.
* Vince medically withdrawn; moves home.
* Cantwell hearing (~wk 40) — he testifies; commitment upheld.
* The date — Theresa books the Greystone. “I had fun / me too” hours later.
* Swearing-in invitation arrives via interoffice mail.
* Christmas Eve: he stays home from mass; Theresa goes alone. The mass program reaches the drawer via her grocery list on the back. (Scored moment.)
* One bourbon alone in the office. Hendersons dinner.
* Hartman running long underneath.
dec.notes: Calendar: the swearing-in and the wedding date are on it, but the surrounding weeks have less filled in — visible gaps in the ink where he stopped and came back days later.

jan.events:
Weeks 43–46 — swearing-in, Vince back, the letter.
* Vince at the kitchen table. Notebook: “V. won’t look at me.” (Scored moment — two pages from a note of full professional competence.)
* Theresa’s swearing-in (wk 44) — he’s not fully present.
* Cantwell’s “letter from the facility” arrives (wk 44).
* Gianna at breakfast: “Dad, are you sleeping?”
* Brandt review (wk 45).
* Theresa’s text (wk 45): “Made appointment for V. with Dr. Hahn. Wednesday.” He doesn’t reply.
* Eva’s crescendo begins: physical alone (wk 44), a dated commitment (wk 45), mornings reclaimed (wk 46).
jan.notes: Calendar thinner — single-word entries: court, eval. Some crossed out without rescheduled dates. Notebook for week 43 nearly empty.

feb.events:
Weeks 47–50 — bathroom leak, final Eva, wedding, grenade.
* Hartman trails off, handed to counsel, unresolved.
* Eva fixes the bathroom leak herself (wk 47). Notebook: “V. laughed once.”
* Eva wk 48 — calm, integrated; “Cautiously optimistic.” A true read.

== Wedding week (week 49) ==
* Mon–Tue: normal work; Sayles discharge note drafted.
* Wed: Eva’s last session — an ordinary Wednesday. “See you next week.”
* Thu: light work. Annabel arrives.
* Fri: rehearsal dinner at the Greystone. Gianna knocks late — “Dad?” Deflection. 11:42 PM, “You okay?” — read, no reply. Eva dies that night.
* Sat: the wedding. Toast draft on the back of the program.
* Sun: quiet.

== Week 50 — Monday, the grenade ==
Theresa’s note in his lunch bag: “You did good Saturday. Love you.” At the office: the clipping, the obituary, [[Connie Howell|Connie]]’s voicemail, the Sayles discharge signed, the unfilable case-closure form, the dated blank page. Part One ends.

Part Two: brittle days Tuesday–Friday. Some morning his hand reaches for the keys. The drive to [[Presque Isle State Park|Presque Isle]].
feb.notes: The load-bearing spread: wedding Saturday, Eva’s last Wednesday, the rehearsal Friday, the never-happened Eva slot the next week. The blank Monday of week 50 sits at the chapter’s opening. Part Two has no calendar.

characters.name: Theresa Messina
characters.occupation: PA State Police — Captain, then Major
characters.summary: Theresa Messina is Anthony’s wife, a Pennsylvania State Police captain promoted to major mid-year. The strongest thing in his life, and the hand he can’t take.
characters.appearance: Gorgeous without working at it. Athletic from running, not the gym. The same hairstyle every morning — a ritual that says exactly who she is. Runs the lake most mornings.
characters.personality: Cool soda on a hot day. Funny, warm, loves to learn; not cynically brilliant. Reads, cooks, runs. Trained to assess the whole room. Suspicious but trusting — knows when something is off and when to wait. They have a pact of not bringing work home; she keeps her side without comment.
characters.backstory: Molly-and-Arthur-Weasley parents: a big, warm, food-and-chaos house. Brunch the last Sunday of every month at her parents’.

sections.title: Narrative access
sections.text: Strictly external — and most powerful where it is almost broken. The reader meets her only through what she sends him: texts, voicemails, notes in his lunch bag, the speech draft, the grocery lists, the swearing-in invitation, the reservation, the birthday card. Her interior stays hers. The strongest moments are where it leaks through the surface (the speech draft; the photo of them looking at each other across the room). Guard those.

sections.title: Arc
sections.text: Rises across the year while he runs at his edge. Promotion lands. She watches him fade. She reaches — text, call, the “Are you okay?”, the “?”. She doesn’t escalate because she trusts him as an adult. That trust is part of what makes his collapse cruel: she has given him room to come back, and he can’t.

sections.title: The final day
sections.text:
A morning call she places (unanswered). She tries to catch him at the house and misses by ten minutes. Texts as the day goes on. The missed calls at 19:30, 22:41 and 22:43 are hers.

In a private moment in Part Two she says his given name — ''Anthony'' — the first and only time the reader hears it. He registers it. He does not respond.

mar.events:
Grocery list on the back of a PA State Police memo: eggs / bread / G’s lunch / coffee filters / call my mother.
Voicemail: “Picking up V’s stuff at 5. Gas in your truck. Love you.”

jul.events: Takes the promotional exam. Her fatal-accident day (wk 20): “I’m OK.” Post-it in his lunch bag.

sep.events: The vacation: “Should I book it?” — no reply.

dec.events: Books the Greystone for a date — “I had fun / me too.” Christmas Eve mass alone; her grocery list on the back of the program.

jan.events: Sworn in as Major (wk 44). Makes the Dr. Hahn appointment for Vince: “Wednesday.” (wk 45) — no reply from him.

feb.events: Rehearsal dinner and the wedding (wk 49). Monday wk 50: “You did good Saturday. Love you.” in his lunch bag. The final day: the unanswered morning call, missing him at the house by ten minutes, the calls at 19:30, 22:41, 22:43.

characters.personality: Mommy’s boy. The Sunday-caller. The big brother the other three actually call.
characters.voice: Warm, dry-witted. Texts in full sentences.

facts.value: Awful — looks like a doctor’s prescription

sections.title: Arc

characters.name: Claire Messina
characters.summary: Claire Messina is the second Messina child, a pre-med senior at [[Gannon University]] in Erie, drifting quietly from the faith.
characters.personality: Mario Kart speedrunner. Optimisation-minded, quick, slightly obsessive. The faith drift is real but not dramatic; an agnostic boyfriend is pulling her quietly out of practice.
characters.voice: Quick. Dry. Affectionate but careful. Rare calls; one voicemail when something mattered.

facts.label: Hand
facts.value: Bubbly (hearts dotting her i’s) but structurally typed-clean

sections.title: Arc
sections.text: Thin on purpose — the drifting daughter whose father didn’t engage with the drift. Missed Easter call. No cross at her throat (Theresa notices first). Med-school essay emailed to Anthony for review — he opens it nine days late. A visit home: mass without communion. Decides on a gap year before med school; Anthony supportive but distant on the call.

characters.name: Vincent Messina
characters.summary: Vincent “Vinny” Messina is the third Messina child, a hockey-playing sophomore at [[Penn State Behrend]] — the son least like his father.
characters.appearance: Lean, mullet, backwards hat, kinda filthy.
characters.personality: Hands, not words. Takes after his grandfather (the carpenter). Loyal, slow-spoken, embarrassed by anything sincere.
characters.voice: One-word texts. Texts only, maybe one or two calls.

facts.label: Hand
facts.value: Unintelligible; prints when he has to

By the wedding he’s functional: the suit fits, he hugs Joey at the reception, dances once with Gianna.

nov.events: Concussion (wk 35; ER fax). Week 37: not better.

characters.name: Gianna Messina
characters.summary: Gianna Messina is the youngest Messina child, a senior at [[Our Lady of Immaculate Conception]] — the witness.
characters.personality: Neurodivergent — reads as autistic without anyone in the family making a thing of it. Pattern recognition that makes her see what no one else does. Misses some social cues, catches others sharper than anyone in the room. Keep her a full kid (prom, essays, the hurt of the broken promise) — a person who happens to notice, never a noticing-device with a backstory.
characters.voice: Direct. Asks questions without softening them.

sections.title: Arc
sections.text: College essays. Acceptance letters in spring. Prom in April. The broken promise (October — “tomorrow morning, promise”; the essay sits on his desk for months). Witness moments: “Vince hasn’t eaten. Going to bring him toast” (wk 38), “Dad, are you sleeping?” at breakfast (wk 44), “You okay?” at 11:42 PM, week 49 — read, no reply.

nov.events: “Vince hasn’t eaten. Going to bring him toast.” (wk 38)

feb.events: Friday of wedding week: knocks late — “Dad?” Deflection. 11:42 PM: “You okay?” — read, no reply. Dances once with Vince at the wedding.

characters.name: Eva Miller
characters.summary: Eva Miller is a post-attempt mandate patient Anthony sees from week 26 until the Friday night of week 49. She was making it — until one morning she wasn’t. The grenade.
characters.appearance: Krysten Ritter in ''Jessica Jones''. Not a 10, not bad. Freckles. Hair always a wreck. The face of a woman who has worked twelve-hour shifts since seventeen.
characters.backstory: Hard childhood. Out at 23. Met [[Aubrey Schultz|Aubrey]] at 28; ten years together. Aubrey was diagnosed about ten months before the book opens and died three months later. Eva’s attempt came about five months before the book opens.

sections.title: Narrative access
sections.text: Opaque. She isn’t special — she’s a patient. The reader meets her only through Anthony’s clinical filter, the same instrument that couldn’t save her. No transcript moment, no document of her own. The reader fails to read her as he failed.

sections.title: Death
sections.text:
Friday night, week 49. Discovered Saturday morning; the obituary lists Friday. The same night Gianna’s “you okay?” text to Anthony goes unanswered at 11:42 PM. Two people reached for him that night. He answered neither. No causal link is drawn — they share only a clock.

See [[Eva’s locked arc]].

sections.title: Function
sections.text: The patient he could not save. The grenade. The win that was real. The book does not answer whether anything could have been seen, because there was nothing to see.

characters.talk:
== To decide ==
* Week 45 — pick ONE concrete, dated forward commitment: Connie putting her back on the Sunday rotation; the grief group continuing through summer; or a standing thing with a coworker.

aug.events: Intake (wk 26). Hospital-hold paperwork from UPMC; 72-hour hold documentation; mandated outpatient referral. Intake questionnaire in her handwriting. PHQ-9 (severe), PCL-5 (significant). First session note — 2–4 pages. Margin: ''guarded. compliant. flat affect appropriate to recent loss.''

sep.events: Early sessions (wks 27–29): Aubrey’s story in pieces. The diner. Connie. Week 30 — the first positive marker: the middle-of-bed sleep change. “Pt. reports change in sleep arrangement. Affect appropriate.”

oct.events: Steady work. Grief group joined. Clothes donated in batches.

nov.events: Coffee for one. The cat. “Concrete grief work continuing.” By the late 30s she is unmistakably climbing; Anthony allows himself “cautiously optimistic” in a margin — and he is right to.

jan.events:
* Wk 44 — annual physical, alone: the first time without Aubrey on speakerphone in eleven years. Bloodwork; a spring follow-up booked. Margin: “first independent medical. — milestone.”
* Wk 45 — a forward commitment with a date (to decide). No margin.
* Wk 46 — mornings reclaimed: waking earlier, walks before her shift. Margin: “sleep cycle adjusting. mornings tolerated.”

feb.events:
* Wk 47 — the apartment kept: calls the plumber herself about the bathroom leak; files her tax return alone.
* Wk 48 — the plateau. “Pt. calm and integrated. Sleep stable. Affect appropriate. Cautiously optimistic.” A true read.
* Wk 49, Wednesday — the last session. Ordinary in every direction. A diner customer who reminded her of someone; she laughed about it. “See you next week.”
* Friday night, wk 49 — she dies.
feb.notes: Monday wk 50: the clipping, the obituary (a brother and a mother she barely spoke to; Aubrey absent), Connie’s voicemail, the unfilable case-closure form.

characters.name: Aubrey Schultz
characters.summary: Aubrey Schultz was [[Eva Miller]]’s partner of ten years, a NICU nurse at [[UPMC Hamot]] who died of pancreatic cancer three months after diagnosis. The reason; the whole loss.
characters.appearance: Quiet, gentle, soft. Lovely without vanity. (Keep description restrained — she is a holy absence; hyperbole sits wrong against the book’s reticence.)
characters.backstory: Beloved by families at Hamot. Unmarried partners with Eva; possibly excluded from Aubrey’s hospital room at the end by Aubrey’s family. Pancreatic cancer — three months from diagnosis to death, about seven months before the book opens.

sections.title: In the archive
sections.text: Eva’s intake form lists Aubrey’s death as the precipitating loss. She appears in session notes by name and phrase. Possibly one photograph in the file. The coffee maker in Eva’s kitchen is one she bought.

characters.name: Raffaella Zanella
characters.summary: Raffaella “Raffi” Zanella has run Anthony’s front desk for seven years — scheduling, billing, the door.
characters.personality: A pro. Holds her own. Takes shit about candle orders without flinching. Reads him too well to perform. Probably one of the first people to notice something is wrong — and says nothing for months, because it isn’t her place.

facts.label: Hand
facts.value: Brisk handwritten Post-its on files; texts in efficient bursts

facts.label: Names
facts.value: “Raffaella” on documents · “Raffi” in his texts and Post-its

sections.title: The two names
sections.text: “Raffaella” on documents (email signature, office letterhead, billing line); “Raffi” in his texts and on the Post-its he writes to her. The shift between the two registers across the record marks the distance between professional and familiar.

sections.title: Role in the ending
sections.text: She transcribes incoming voicemails for the file — including [[Connie Howell|Connie]]’s after Eva’s death — and places the Monday clipping on his desk. In Part Two she reschedules silently.

feb.events: Monday wk 50: places the clipping on his desk; transcribes Connie’s voicemail for the file. Then reschedules silently through the brittle days.

characters.summary: Annabel Coster is [[Joey Messina|Joey]]’s fiancée, the daughter of a wealthy Protestant farming family in Ohio.

characters.name: Connie Howell
characters.summary: Connie Howell has owned [[Connie’s]] diner for more than thirty years and treats [[Eva Miller|Eva]] like a daughter.

sections.title: The voicemail
sections.text:
Monday afternoon of week 50, transcribed by Raffaella for the file:

''“It’s Connie. Just wanted to let you know about Eva. Thank you for what you tried to do. I’m here if you want to call.”''

Anthony doesn’t.

feb.events: Monday of week 50: leaves Anthony a voicemail about Eva. He doesn’t call.

characters.name: Anthony’s father
characters.summary: Anthony’s father is a carpenter — stable, nurturing — now at [[Lake Arthur Retirement Village]]. Vince takes after him.

sections.title: In the book

characters.name: Anthony’s mother
characters.summary: Anthony’s mother was a military JAG investigator — forensic by training, principled and methodical. He is her son in a different forensic discipline.

sections.title: In the book
sections.text: One voicemail auto-transcript garbles her accent into nonsense; he saves the voicemail anyway.

characters.name: Marcus Wayne Reeves
characters.summary: Marcus Reeves is the opening case: a 19-year-old evaluated for competency to stand trial on a criminal-homicide charge. He reads competent on the surface; Anthony sees the concealed trauma underneath — and is right.

sections.title: Function
sections.text: Calibrates the reader to the form and to his eye — when this man says he sees something, he sees it. A structural opener, not a thematic one. Reeves never points at Eva.

sections.title: Intake session note
sections.text:
The sample note from the plan. Clinical default in the body; his real voice in the marginalia. The marginalia dated 3/14 — six days later — show him returning to the file. 
SESSION NOTE
Patient:    Marcus Reeves
DOB:        [redacted] (19 y/o)
Eval type:  Competency to stand trial — Dusky standard
Date:       March 8, 2030
Session:    1 (intake)
Examiner:   A. Messina, MD
Duration:   90 min.

PRESENTING:
Pt. is a 19-y/o Cauc. male, jail-referred per court order
[ref #] for CST eval. Index charge: criminal homicide,
single victim (stepfather, age 47). Pt. presents oriented
x3, jail-issued attire, calm, cooperative. Eye contact
appropriate. Affect mildly constricted, appropriate to
setting. Speech normal rate and volume. Thought process
linear. No evidence of psychosis. No SI/HI reported.
Denies prior MH treatment.

HISTORY:
Pt. relates childhood across multiple states — Ohio,
Indiana, Kentucky, returning to PA at age 11. On direct:
"we moved a lot." Asked re: reason, pt. shrugged. "My
mom worked different places." Asked re: schools, pt.
named four elementary schools before age 11. After age
11, one middle school, one high school.

[Marginalia, blue pen, undated:
 11 is the age the moves stopped.]

Family of origin: biological mother (alive, currently
employed as a hospital aide); biological father
(estranged, last contact age 8); stepfather (decedent,
married mother when pt. was 9 or 10 — pt. uncertain).
One younger half-sibling (age 14, currently with mother).

On the stepfather: pt. described relationship as "around."
Asked to elaborate, pt. paused. Eventually: "He wasn't
gone." Asked if relationship was good or bad, pt. said
"depends what day." Asked to give an example, pt. said
"every day was a different day." Asked re: physical
discipline: pt. said "regular stuff."

[Marginalia, blue pen, dated 3/14:
 "regular stuff" — clarify, follow up if M-eval ordered.]

Asked re: head trauma: pt. denied. On second pass: pt.
described a fall at age 13 "from the porch." Asked if
medically treated: no. Asked re: duration of LOC: "I
don't know, my mom said I was up." Asked re: residual
symptoms: denied. (ER records pending — requesting.)

[Marginalia, blue pen, dated 3/14:
 "from the porch" — no further detail. He said it like
 someone reciting a date. Look at the records.]

EDUCATION:
Inconsistent attendance pre-11; consistent post-11. Pt.
graduated regular diploma, no special ed. Pt. reports
B-/C+ average. No detentions of note. One in-school
suspension (unspecified). No work history beyond seasonal
landscaping.

SUBSTANCE USE:
Pt. denies regular use of alcohol or illicit substances.
Reports first alcohol at 15 (parent's house), occasional
use since. Marijuana: tried 2x. No nicotine.

LEGAL HISTORY:
No prior arrests. No juvenile record. No civil involvement.

EVENT (per pt.'s account, summarized):
Pt. relates the incident in a flat, sequential manner.
Pt. states he came home from work, found stepfather and
mother in argument; pt. intervened verbally; stepfather
struck mother; pt. struck stepfather. Pt. does not
describe the weapon or its use. When asked, pt. paused,
then: "I'm not supposed to talk about that part."
(Counsel's instruction appropriate; not pursued.)

MENTAL STATUS — competency-relevant:
Pt. articulate; understands the nature of charges;
demonstrates familiarity with court roles. Can recite
his attorney's name. Demonstrates capacity to assist
counsel via concrete answers re: factual questions.
Affect appropriate to gravity. Reality testing intact.
No malingering indicators (instrument results pending).

CLINICAL IMPRESSION:
Pt. meets the Dusky standard for competency to stand
trial. He understands the nature and consequences of
the proceedings against him and is able to consult with
his attorney with a reasonable degree of rational
understanding.

However.

[Marginalia, blue pen, dated 3/14:
 "every day was a different day"
 "regular stuff"
 "from the porch"
 He told me three things on intake. The moves stopped
 at 11. The fall at 13. The stepfather is dead. He told
 me these things in order. He told me without being
 asked. He has been thinking about this order for a
 long time.]

RECOMMENDATION:
1. Competency to stand trial — AFFIRMED.
2. Strongly recommend mitigation evaluation prior to
   disposition.
3. Request: complete school, medical, child welfare
   records.
4. Defense counsel should be made aware of likely
   significant childhood trauma history not captured
   in original intake.

DISPOSITION:
Report to be issued to [court], [DA], [defense counsel]
within 14 days. Follow-up: not required for competency.
Mitigation eval recommended (separate referral).

A. Messina, MD
[Signature]

articles.name: As the Moon Swallows the Stars
articles.summary: ''As the Moon Swallows the Stars'' is Book 1 of a trilogy: a literary tragedy (70,000+ words) told as the contents of forensic psychiatrist [[Anthony Messina]]’s working desk drawer across one year, March 2030 to February 2031 — until the man closes the drawer and the form breaks into prose.

sections.title: The seed line
sections.text:
The book’s originating line, which becomes the closing line:

''As the moon swallowed the stars, I realized — we were all alone.''
— A. M.

The line is precise rather than Romantic. The moon doesn’t destroy the stars. It makes them invisible. They’re still there; the brightness of the moon outshines them. That’s what suicidal depression is — the lights of your life don’t go out; they’re outshone by the overwhelming pull. Theresa is still there. The kids are still there. The work is still there. You can’t see them. The moon is too bright.

The title is the present tense of the line. The reader holds the title for 350 pages, watching the swallowing happen slowly. The closing line is when Anthony sees it has happened.

sections.title: Concept and form
sections.text:
The book is the literal contents of Dr. Anthony Messina’s working desk drawer across a single year — typed case notes, handwritten annotations, Post-its, court orders, intake forms and questionnaires, standardised screening inventories, phone screenshots, voicemail transcripts, text exchanges, emails, calendar pages, GPS screenshots, his personal pocket notebook, newspaper clippings, an obituary, a few photos, receipts, permission slips, postcards, a grocery list, a swearing-in invitation.

Each page is a discrete document, interleaved in roughly chronological order. The clinical work is the spine; life material is shuffled in around it.

'''The drawer is metaphor.''' It is the organising frame, not a real container. (See [[The form contract]].)

Part One ends with the news of Eva’s death reaching him — clipping, obituary, the unfilable case-closure form, a dated blank page. Part Two is third-person close, free indirect, ~30 pages of pure descent. The final page returns to facsimile: a piece of lined paper from his notebook, his handwriting, one line, his initial.

sections.title: The shape
sections.text:
Three movements, but the middle one is invisible until it isn’t.

== The condition (weeks 1–49) ==
Anthony has been at the edge of his capacity for years. He doesn’t know it. The work product stays excellent; the life product thins. The reader watches this and doesn’t quite know they’re watching. On page 100 they see grocery lists. By page 200 they don’t, and don’t notice the absence. By page 300 they vaguely remember Theresa used to write him grocery lists and aren’t sure when that stopped.

== The grenade (week 50) ==
[[Eva Miller|Eva]] dies. She was cautiously optimistic. She was doing the work. She was, in fact, making it — until one morning she wasn’t. The grenade ends his ability to hold the imbalance. He doesn’t crumble because Eva broke him. He crumbles because what was already true becomes visible.

== The fall (weeks 50–51) ==
Quiet emptying. He goes home. He returns to the office. He cannot pick up the work. Some morning his hand reaches for the keys. The drive. The beach.

The parallelism: both Eva and Anthony might have lived. Anthony failed to see Eva. The system failed to see Anthony. The book holds both questions open and answers neither.

sections.title: Two parts
sections.text:
== Part One: The Archive (weeks 1–50, ~320 pages) ==
Page one through the news of Eva’s death. His condition is never narrated — it is inferred from absences in the documentary record. The wedding lands as a document cluster (week 49 Saturday). Eva dies Friday night, week 49; Anthony attends the wedding not knowing; Monday of week 50 the clipping arrives. Part One ends with:
* News clipping
* Obituary
* Connie’s voicemail (transcribed by Raffaella)
* The unfilable case-closure form
* The dated blank page

== Part Two: The Slide Bottoms (~30 pages) ==
Third-person close, free indirect, set in a serif literary face (Garamond, Sabon, Caslon). Pure descent. The drive appears as one final document — an Apple Maps screenshot, home to [[Presque Isle State Park|Presque Isle]]: ''Now departing. 1 hr 26 min.'' The beach, ~8–12 pages, adagio.

The ending is ambiguous, tilted toward suicide but not stated. He could die of exposure on the truck. He could drive home at 4 AM. The book refuses to tell. See [[Part Two beat sheet]].

sections.title: The closing
sections.text:
The book closes on the same hand it opened with — but unable to file itself. The last real thing is not furniture; it is a document that cannot complete itself. The recovery checkbox cannot be checked over a dead woman. The line is written in the wrong hand, outside the box. The page is dated, signed, unfilable. The form’s final act of containment is to record its own failure, and then the narrator stops watching.

The reader does the rest.

sections.title: The trilogy
sections.text: A triptych of working lives; any connection between the three is coincidental and authorial, never in-world. Book 2, ''Across the Bridge'' (Bugatti — unmoved). Book 3, ''Captain Wynn'' (Wynn — sustained). “Salt and Glass,” once floated as the Book 3 title, is now the name of Wynn’s fifth case.

articles.name: The iron rules
articles.summary: The iron rules are the seven philosophical commitments the book holds across every page. Rules 1, 2 and 6 are governed by [[The form contract]].

sections.title: The seven rules
sections.text:
# '''Form is character — meaning the gap, not the surface.''' The form is his armoured, performed self: the part most rewarded, most practised, kept immaculate by will. Character lives in the distance between the clean surface and the absences around it.
# '''Presence through artifact — until the artifact fails.''' Anthony is never directly described. He is built from what he produced, kept, annotated, chose to save. Part Two is the engineered exception: the access is the ''failure'' of this rule, not its suspension.
# '''The slide is absence, not degradation.''' The work product stays him; the slide is in what he stops doing. Family goes first. Friends second. Self third. Work last.
# '''The reader has equal access and equal blindness.''' Anthony logs every echo and connects none of them. The book’s deepest grief — ''was it catchable, or was there nothing to catch'' — must remain genuinely unanswered. There is no planted tell.
# '''No villain. No mechanism. No turn.''' The case ends because grief is grief. The convergence is the only force.
# '''One point of access — and the form breaks to grant it.''' Never inside anyone but Anthony, and inside Anthony only when the form has failed. Theresa stays external. Eva stays opaque.
# '''Professionalism is not cynicism.''' Anthony is still trying when she dies. That is what makes it tragedy. The book is not satire.

articles.name: The form contract
articles.summary: The form contract states where the form is allowed to break, and why each break is an event rather than an error. The form is a containment: it holds the man the way his professionalism holds him — completely, until it doesn’t.

sections.title: The drawer is metaphor. Fully. Throughout.
sections.text: The drawer is never a literal container the reader is asked to picture. There is no scene of a physical drawer. Consequence for the close: the ending cannot rest on a physical drawer; it rests on a ''document'' that cannot file itself. The power is in the paper, never the furniture.

sections.title: Part Two is a rupture of single-access. On purpose.
sections.text: For 320 pages the book never gets inside him. Part Two gets inside him for thirty. The documents could contain the man as long as the man held. When he comes apart, the containment fails. The reader should feel the floor drop.

sections.title: What the Part Two narration is made of
sections.text:
Not a new omniscience switched on at the end: the forensic gaze itself — the same external, clinical watching Anthony has aimed at other people for twenty-five years — finally turned on its operator. It observes him from outside, behaviourally, refusing interiority. It can watch him to the waterline and no further.

The single first-person utterance is the subject speaking back to the gaze — the only moment in the book the watched man says ''I''. The rupture has a rupture.

sections.title: The seam between the parts
sections.text: The unfilable case-closure form is the hinge. It is the last thing the archive can hold — the form’s final successful act of containment is to record its own failure. Part One ends on it as document (then the dated blank page, the held breath). Part Two opens at the same desk, the same Monday, in prose: the pen just set down, the form already complete behind him. The repetition of the moment across two registers ''is'' the rupture.

sections.title: What “form is character” actually claims
sections.text: It does not mean the surface decays with the self. The surface ''is'' the armoured, performed self, and character lives in the gap between that clean surface and the absences accumulating around it. The form doesn’t degrade because ''he'' wouldn’t let it. That refusal is the portrait.

articles.name: Physical form
articles.summary: How the book is built as an object: the drawer, the document types, the calendar spreads, the handwriting registers and the date stamps.

sections.title: Document types
sections.text:
== The clinical bulk ==
* Typed case notes (clean sans-serif, 1–4 pages depending on session type)
* Intake questionnaires (multi-page forms, patient’s handwriting in boxes)
* Screening inventories — PHQ-9, GAD-7, PCL-5, HCR-20, MMPI-2-RF
* Court referral packets (letterhead, court order, charge summary)
* Records release forms; court filings; deposition transcripts
* Recorded forensic interview transcripts (rare)
* Full eval reports

== Life detritus ==
* Phone screenshots (call history, missed calls, voicemail rows)
* Text messages; emails
* Calendar pages (two-page spreads as chapter breaks)
* GPS screenshots (commutes, court drives, the drive to the beach)
* Voicemail auto-transcripts
* Receipts, postcards, permission slips, grocery lists, prom photos, report cards, Christmas-card photos, mass programs, ticket stubs

== The pocket Moleskine ==
Three days per page, bullets, blue pen, ruled paper. Sloppy — the honest mode. Degrades by thinning: daily, weekly, monthly; some weeks no entries.

sections.title: Voicemails
sections.text:
The natural document form for missed calls, in iPhone Visual Voicemail layout: sender, date/time, duration, listened/unlistened, auto-transcribed text. Early in the year, two or three short ones, all listened. Late year, six or seven, several unlistened. The ''Unread'' indicator is its own document.
* Theresa: daily morning call; voicemails when missed, increasingly often
* Joey: weekend calls
* Vince: texts only; maybe one or two calls
* Claire: rare calls; one voicemail when something mattered
* Gianna: in person
* His parents: 1–2 calls from Lake Arthur; one transcript garbles his mother’s accent into nonsense and he saves it anyway

sections.title: The notes are alive
sections.text:
Clinical notes are working documents — typed, then revised by hand across the year: crossed-out passages, dated marginal annotations in different inks, arrows, circles, asterisks. A March note read in March has no marginalia yet; when it becomes relevant in October, he adds an October-dated annotation and puts it back. What changes is which files he goes back to, and how often.

* Intake notes: 2–4 pages, dense, direct quotes, marginalia accumulating
* Follow-ups: one page or less — Since last session / Mental status / Themes / Plan

sections.title: Weekly rhythm
sections.text: Roughly per week: 3–4 session notes; 1 calendar page (the month’s chapter break); 1–3 life documents; 0–1 notebook entries; 0–2 voicemails; 1–3 questionnaires. Across 52 weeks, about 350–400 pages.

sections.title: The calendar as chapter break
sections.text:
Each chapter is a two-page spread of one month’s calendar — twelve across the book. The calendars are the planning self, not the executing self: he plans each month at the end of the prior one, and the gap between calendar-Anthony and document-Anthony is the slide.
* '''March–July:''' dense, clean, every weekday filled, planned in one sitting, clean fountain-pen hand
* '''August–September:''' dense, still clean; Eva’s standing appointment absorbed
* '''October–November:''' slight gaps; the first ''?'' beside a Sunday brunch
* '''December:''' swearing-in and wedding date on it; surrounding weeks thinner; visible gaps in the ink
* '''January:''' thinner; single-word entries — ''court'', ''eval''; entries crossed out without new dates
* '''February:''' the load-bearing spread — wedding Saturday, Eva’s last Wednesday, the rehearsal Friday, the never-happened Eva slot; the blank Monday of week 50

The deeper degradation is the visible loss of advance-planning capacity. '''Part Two has no calendar.''' See [[Calendar spread]].

sections.title: Visual hierarchy
sections.text: Three handwriting fonts minimum — Anthony (clinical, marginalia, notebook), Theresa, child/other. A few institutional fonts; typewriter or clean sans for case notes; a serif form font for legal documents; a newsprint face for clippings. Seven or eight registers. Every document carries a date in a small consistent typeface — the reader’s compass. See [[Style sheet]].

sections.title: Part Two — the visual collapse
sections.text: A single page with only the date of Eva’s death. Otherwise blank. The held breath. Then prose in serif type. No header. The reader simply turns the page and finds a novel. The last page returns to facsimile: lined notebook paper, his hand, one line, ''— A. M.''

sections.title: Production
sections.text:
Twelve hand-rendered calendar spreads, multiple handwriting registers, photos, programs, receipts, voicemail screenshots. Achievable in B&W on standard literary stock; for an elevated edition, limited two-colour (blue ink for the notebook).

'''Production is not deferrable.''' The production model ''is'' the artwork. Cost, price point, handwriting consistency across 350 pages and near-impossibility as an ebook are identity questions, not logistics.

articles.name: Voice and register
articles.summary: How Anthony sounds in each mode of Part One, the rules for Part Two’s prose, and the book’s few scored moments.

sections.title: Part One — the documents speak
sections.text:
* '''Typed clinical notes''' — clean sans-serif, professional vocabulary, lapsed-Catholic syntax flickering under stress (''However.'' standing alone)
* '''Marginal annotations''' — blue pen, dated, conservative
* '''Pocket notebook''' — blue pen, ruled paper, sloppy, the honest mode

Clinical default in the body, his real voice in the marginalia. The gap between the typed line and the penciled line is the book. See the sample intake note on [[Marcus Reeves]] and the notebook samples on [[Anthony Messina]].

sections.title: Part Two — third-person close
sections.text:
Adagio. Slow, patient, no quick beats. After 300 pages of dense documents, the prose is the silence after the noise.

'''Rule:''' no sentence names what he is thinking or feeling. No ''he thought'', no ''he realized'', no ''he felt''. The interior verb arrives once, in the closing line.

What carries the interior work:
* Behaviour — what he does, what his hand reaches for
* Dialogue — to Raffaella, to Theresa, to himself under his breath
* Concrete objects — the phone buzzing, the cracking leather chair, the pen he hates, the cold
* Memory as intrusion — a photo on the desk, a song, his father’s hands at a wedding forty years ago
* Vocabulary leakage — ''The keyboard wouldn’t wake up. He smacked it. Fucking thing.''

sections.title: Theresa’s name lands once
sections.text: She says his given name — ''Anthony'' — once in Part Two. The book has held it back for three hundred pages. The release of the name is the release of his interior to her, and his inability to take her hand.

# Christmas Eve mass — the absence; the program reaches the drawer via her grocery list

articles.name: Eva’s locked arc
articles.summary: Eva’s locked arc is the recovery crescendo from week 26 to week 49 (~24 sessions). The win is real. There is no planted tell. The reader must finish week 48 believing she is safe — because Anthony does, because she is.

sections.title: Design principle
sections.text:
Each late marker is a future being built. Future-orientation is the clinical signature of recovery and the cruelest thing a death can take. The height of the fall is measured in how many next-weeks she is holding when the morning comes that she isn’t. Build the futures high.

This is where rules 4 and 5 are kept: a rereader finds only an ordinary Wednesday, which is exactly what was there.

sections.title: Weeks 26–38
sections.text:
* '''Wk 26 — intake.''' UPMC hospital-hold paperwork; mandated outpatient referral; intake questionnaire in her hand; PHQ-9 severe; PCL-5 significant. Margin: ''guarded. compliant. flat affect appropriate to recent loss.''
* '''Wks 27–29.''' Aubrey’s story in pieces. The diner. Connie.
* '''Wk 30 — first positive marker.''' Middle-of-bed sleep change.
* '''Wks 31–38.''' Grief group; clothes donated in batches; coffee for one; the cat. ''Concrete grief work continuing.'' “Cautiously optimistic” in a margin — and he is right to.

sections.title: The crescendo
sections.text:
* '''Wk 44 — the body, forward.''' Annual physical alone; spring follow-up booked. Margin: “first independent medical. — milestone.”
* '''Wk 45 — a commitment with a date.''' Pick ONE, concrete, dated. No margin — a person rejoining time.
* '''Wk 46 — mornings reclaimed.''' Walks before her shift. Margin: “sleep cycle adjusting. mornings tolerated.” (“Tolerated” never gets the upgrade to “reclaimed.”)
* '''Wk 47 — the apartment kept.''' The leak fixed herself; tax return filed alone.
* '''Wk 48 — the plateau.''' “Pt. calm and integrated. Sleep stable. Affect appropriate. Cautiously optimistic.” A TRUE READ.
* '''Wk 49, Wednesday — the last session: ordinary.''' The slightly hurried hand is his distraction, never a tell. “See you next week.” She has a next week. So does he.

sections.title: After
sections.text:
* '''Friday night, wk 49''' — she dies. Not shown. Gianna’s 11:42 PM text goes unanswered the same night.
* '''Saturday''' — discovered. Anthony attends the wedding not knowing.
* '''Monday, wk 50''' — the clipping (plain factual lede), placed by Raffaella. The obituary (a brother and a mother she barely spoke to; Aubrey absent). Connie’s voicemail.
* '''The unfilable file''' — a draft case-closure form, the recovery checkbox hovered over and not completed, the line outside the box in the wrong hand: ''Eva Miller hanged herself in her room.'' Dated. (“Hanged” — locked. The form fails on its content, not its grammar.)
* '''The dated blank page.''' End of Part One.

sections.title: Sequencing for non-pattern
sections.text:
Scatter the resolutions so no two adjacent files end the same way: Reeves affirms-with-a-shadow (Q1), Brandt resolves into nothing (Q1, recurring), Kessler is a clean catch (Q2), Petrak turns and restores (Q3), Cantwell grinds toward a hearing (Q3), Allbright renders a finding (Q3), the ghost case ends in a death nobody annotates (wk 38), Hartman trails off (Q4), Sayles discharges clean (wk 50) — then Eva.

Affirm, null, win, turn, grind, finding, quiet death, trail-off, clean win, then the body. The reader never finds a rhythm, so never learns to brace.

sections.text:

== Week 49 — wedding week ==
* Mon–Tue: normal work; Sayles discharge drafted
* Wed: Eva #24, her last — an ordinary Wednesday; “See you next week.”
* Thu: light work; Annabel arrives
* Fri: rehearsal dinner at the Greystone; Gianna knocks late — “Dad?”; 11:42 PM “You okay?” — read, no reply. Eva dies.
* Sat: the wedding

== Week 50 — Monday: the grenade ==
Theresa’s lunch-bag note. The office. Clipping. Obituary. Connie’s voicemail. Sayles discharge signed. The unfilable case-closure form. The dated blank page. Part One ends.

sections.title: The wedding — document cluster
sections.text:
Week 49, Saturday. * Suit alterations receipt * Wedding program (Catholic mass, Father [name]) * Toast draft on the back of the program, multiple versions struck through * Group-chat flood of photos that evening — Joey and Anthony forehead-to-forehead on the dance floor; Anthony looking across the room at Theresa, Theresa looking back * Reception bar tab 
Version 1 (struck through):
  "From the moment Joey was born I knew this day
  would —"

Version 2 (struck through):

Version 3 (mostly struck through, one line saved):

  [strikethrough]"

Final, clean:
  "My son was always going to find someone good.
  I'm grateful she found him too. To Joey and

articles.summary: The opening week is a sequence of 13 documents establishing form, family, work and voice. By page 12–15 the reader knows the form, the family, the marriage, the work, his voice and his clinical eye.

# Text exchange, Anthony to Vince: “good luck today” / “thx old man”

articles.name: Part Two beat sheet
articles.summary: Part Two: ~30 pages of pure descent. Third-person close, free indirect, adagio — the forensic gaze turned on its operator.

sections.title: Opening — Monday morning at the office
sections.text: The prose picks up in the immediate aftermath of the unfilable form; it does not re-enact the writing. Voice: brittle, irritable. The obituary printed. The pen just set down. The recovery checkbox not completed. He gets up. Goes home.

sections.title: The days — Tuesday through Friday
sections.text: Brittle days. The Sayles discharge note signed Tuesday or Wednesday. A few sessions. Raffaella rescheduling silently. By Thursday he can’t pick up the work. By Friday the office is effectively closed. In a private moment, Theresa says ''Anthony''. He registers it. He does not respond.

sections.title: The drive — some morning
sections.text: His hand reaches for the keys. The GPS screenshot — ''Now departing. 1 hr 26 min.'' — the one document in the prose section. Time slips; memory and present share paragraphs. A toll booth and his father’s hands at a wedding forty years ago. The wipers. Theresa’s missed calls. Gianna’s college essay unopened on his desk for six months.

sections.title: The beach — afternoon into night
sections.text:
[[Presque Isle State Park|Presque Isle]]. Open sky. The lake. He climbs on the roof of the truck and lies down. Watches the stars. The phone buzzes: Theresa, 22:41. Again, 22:43. He pulls out the pocket notebook. The pen he hates. He writes the line. He initials it.

== Tilt toward suicide ==
* The phone buzzes and he doesn’t answer
* The pen he hates is the pen he writes with
* The line is in the register of a closing line
* The initial is formal — A. M. with the period. Signed.
* No forward-looking image — no thought of tomorrow, of Theresa waking
* February. Lake Erie. He doesn’t move

== Counter-weights ==
* The keys are still in his pocket. The truck runs.
* A long exhale after the line. A small release.
* He doesn’t get off the truck. Doesn’t walk toward the water.

Cold is the mechanism. Inaction does it. The ambiguity is built into the situation.

sections.title: The closing page — facsimile
sections.text:
Lined paper from his pocket notebook. His handwriting.

''As the moon swallowed the stars, I realized — we were all alone.''
— A. M.

The only first-person utterance in the book — the watched man speaking back to the gaze.

articles.name: Production spec
articles.summary: The production spec (v1): everything decided in session one about how the book is physically made. See also [[Style sheet]], [[Calendar spread]], [[Word setup]] and [[Open items]].

sections.title: The book
sections.text: Anthony Messina’s desk drawer across one year, told as discrete facsimile documents in chronological order. Twelve two-page calendar spreads as chapter breaks. Part One entirely facsimile; after Eva’s death and a nearly blank dated page, ~30 pages of third-person prose; the final page returns to facsimile. Seven or eight visual registers. Three handwriting modes for Anthony alone across 350+ pages.

sections.title: Production method
sections.text:
'''Never round-trip the typed layer.''' Rescanning printed type destroys it — soft edges, halftone artifacts, moiré. The typed layer stays native and vector forever.

== The ink-only overlay workflow ==
# Print the typed page as a ''guide'' at 15–20% grey, or light blue
# Handwrite annotations on it
# Scan at 600 dpi, greyscale, TIFF — auto-enhance and auto-crop OFF
# Levels: pull the white point until the guide and paper vanish, leaving only ink
# Place as a '''Multiply''' layer over the untouched digital page

Variant: print only registration corners and a faint content box, write around it, same knockout.

== Materials ==
Laser prints, not inkjet. Pigment pens (Sakura Micron, Uni Pin) scan crisper than ballpoint. Fountain pen looks right but feathers on laser stock — test first. Flatbed scanner, never phone.

== Handwriting consistency ==
Build custom fonts from your own hand via Calligraphr — one for clinical marginalia, one for the sloppy notebook, one for Theresa — with multiple alternates per letter. Reserve genuine pen-on-paper scans for scored moments: the anniversary receipt, the mass program, the final notebook page.

== Order of operations ==
Write the entire manuscript as tagged plain text FIRST — [SESSION NOTE], [NOTEBOOK], [MARGINALIA — blue, dated]. Lock the text. Then one production pass. Every revision after a page is handwritten and scanned costs an hour.

sections.title: Why 7 × 10
sections.text: In-world documents are US Letter. At 6 × 9 they reproduce at ~55%, turning 10pt clinical type into 5.5pt. At 7 × 10 they’re at ~70%. The calendar spreads also need the width. Design at trim, not at Letter.

sections.title: The safety line
sections.text:
An invisible boundary, not a drawn element — for trim drift (~1/16″, sometimes 1/8″), the gutter curve (~0.25″ each side of the fold) and thumbs on the bottom outer corner. '''Readable content never crosses it. Paper edges may.''' A document’s edge disappearing into the spine reads as a page under another page — what a real stack on a desk looks like.

In Word: View → Ruler; File → Options → Advanced → Show document content → Show text boundaries.

sections.title: Collage logic
sections.text: Most pages combine several small documents — a journal page with a phone call and a text. Major documents (court orders, full case notes) get a page alone, centred and calm. Collage pages feel accumulating; single documents feel formal and isolated.

sections.title: Previewing spreads
sections.text: Word can’t show facing pages correctly (it pairs 1–2, 3–4; a real book pairs 2–3, 4–5). Use '''Firefox''': save as PDF, open it, ">>" → '''Even Spreads''', zoom Actual Size. Make it permanent in about:config: pdfjs.spreadModeOnLoad → 2; pdfjs.defaultZoomValue → 100. Do this after every spread — the only way to catch a Wednesday drifting toward the fold.

articles.name: Word setup
articles.summary: Word setup for drafting and mocking up the typed layer, and the Word behaviours learned the hard way. Final assembly needs Affinity Publisher or InDesign.

sections.title: Document setup
sections.text:
* Layout → Size → 7″ × 10″
* Layout → Margins → Custom → Mirror margins, values per [[Production spec]]
* Page break between documents
* Turn OFF widow/orphan control (except Prose) and snap-to-grid
* File → Options → Save → embed fonts
* Kill autocorrect entirely (both tabs) — it capitalises “pt.”, curls quotes in typewriter documents, converts -- to em dashes, and autocapitalises after “x3.”

sections.title: Hyphenation
sections.text:
* Automatically hyphenate — ON
* Hyphenate words in CAPS — OFF
* Limit consecutive hyphens — 2

Hyphenation Zone is permanently disabled in .docx (engine changed in Word 2013). Ignore it. Per-style ''Don’t hyphenate'' is ON for everything except Newsprint and Prose.

sections.title: Word’s limits
sections.text: No bleed, no CMYK, no Multiply blending. Word handles drafting, register-tagging and mocking up the typed layer. Final assembly: '''Affinity Publisher''' (~$70) or InDesign, set at the same 7 × 10.

sections.title: Behaviours learned the hard way
sections.text:
* '''Paragraph borders merge.''' Consecutive paragraphs with identical borders draw as one block. Different styles, 0.01″ indents and 1-unit colour differences all fail. Use Split Cells instead.
* '''Split Cells locks the Rows field''' with multiple cells selected and “Merge cells before split” unticked. Do cells one at a time.
* '''“Automatically resize to fit contents” is greyed out on nested tables''' — set it on the outer table.
* '''Column widths are stored per row.''' Rows drift after Insert Above; the ¤ markers reveal it. Fix: Fixed Column Width → Distribute Columns → preferred width in inches.
* '''Split Cells produces “At least” row heights.''' Always reset to Exactly.
* '''Ctrl+Enter pushes everything after the cursor.''' Ctrl+Home first.
* '''The ruler reports the cursor’s location''', not the page you’re looking at. Alt+drag a margin marker for exact measurements; Esc before releasing.
* '''Lock anchor blocks dragging the anchor.''' Untick, move, re-tick.
* '''Text boxes carry 0.1″ internal margins''' and float wherever dropped.

articles.name: Style sheet
articles.summary: The style sheet: every paragraph style Based on (no style), Automatically update OFF, Only in this document, line spacing always Exactly.

sections.title: Document registers
sections.text:
* '''Clinical note''' (Ctrl+Alt+1) — Courier New 10, kerning off, left, right indent 0.65″ (a 62-character measure — don’t widen it), exactly 13pt, tabs 1.0″ L, 1.4″ L
* '''Court document''' (Ctrl+Alt+2) — Times New Roman 11, justified, right 0.35″, first line 0.5″, exactly 15pt, tabs 0.5″ L, 1.0″ L, 5.4″ R dot leader
* '''Institutional form''' (Ctrl+Alt+3) — Arial 8.5 condensed 0.1pt, right 0.5″, '''hanging 1.6″''' (what makes a form look like a form), after 3pt, exactly 12pt, tabs 1.6″ L, 5.35″ R underline leader
* '''Newsprint''' (Ctrl+Alt+4) — Georgia 8 condensed 0.15pt, justified, first line 0.14″, exactly 10pt, hyphenation ON; two columns at 1.6″, 0.14″ gutter, hairline rule
* '''Screen''' (Ctrl+Alt+5) — Segoe UI 9, L/R 0.15″, after 2pt, exactly 12pt. Texts, emails, voicemails. Sent bubbles right-aligned 8% grey; received left 3%
* '''Date stamp''' (Ctrl+Alt+6) — Arial 7 all caps, expanded 0.4pt, after 6pt, exactly 9pt, keep with next, followed by Clinical note. Black, not grey — the reader’s compass
* '''Prose''' (Ctrl+Alt+7, Part Two only) — Garamond 11.5, justified, first line 0.2″, exactly 15.5pt, widow/orphan ON, keep lines together ON, hyphenation ON
* '''HAND''' (Ctrl+Alt+8, placeholder, deliberately ugly) — Consolas 10 italic, RGB 0/70/180, L/R 0.25″, before/after 3pt, exactly 12pt. Tag inline: [HAND-marginalia], [HAND-notebook], [HAND-Theresa]

sections.title: Character styles
sections.text:
Set Style type: Character FIRST — switching after entering formatting discards it silently.
* '''Redacted''' — Courier New 10, font colour white; Border → Shading → fill black, apply to Text. Select the word only. Exports reliably to PDF and stays searchable.
* '''Stamp''' — Arial 9 bold, all caps, RGB 150/30/30, expanded 0.6pt. Rotate by putting it in a rotated text box.

sections.title: Variants
sections.text:
* '''Court caption''' — based on Court document; centred, special (none)
* '''Newsprint hed''' — based on Newsprint; Franklin Gothic Demi 15 (Arial Bold fallback), spacing Normal, left, after 4pt, exactly 16pt, don’t hyphenate
* '''Prose opening''' — based on Prose; special (none)

sections.title: Normal as a tripwire
sections.text: Set Normal to Comic Sans MS 14, magenta. All registers are Based on (no style), so they’re immune. Word’s built-ins turn magenta — harmless, but page numbers must be formatted directly. Anything in magenta is untagged text.

sections.title: Template
sections.text: File → Save As → Browse → Word Template (*.dotx) → moon_v1, saved in the project folder, not Custom Office Templates.

articles.talk:
== Open ==

articles.name: Calendar spread
articles.summary: The calendar spread: twelve identical two-page month grids that serve as chapter breaks. Eight columns across the spread; the fold falls between WED and THU.

sections.title: Structure
sections.text:
VERSO                              RECTO
SUN   MON   TUE   WED      |      THU   FRI   SAT   NOTES
Sunday start (the first ''?'' appears beside a Sunday brunch, so Sunday needs full weight). The NOTES column is the eighth column of a uniform grid, not a sidebar — six discrete weekly cells, not one tall box, so the degradation shows week by week.

sections.title: Page parity
sections.text: Page 1 is always a recto. Verso = even; every spread runs even–odd. Leave page 1 blank (half-title) and start March on pp. 2–3. This parity requirement recurs eleven more times as Part One’s document count shifts.

sections.title: Measurements
sections.text:
* Month rule — absolute 0.58″ below Page, 1½pt black
* Day-name row — 0.2″ exactly
* Body rows — 1.38″ × 6 exactly
* Columns — 1.47″ × 4
* Table preferred width — 5.88″
* Writing space per cell — ~1.16″ (3 comfortable lines, 4 cramped)
* NOTES sub-rows — 0.34″ × 4 exactly

sections.title: Calendar styles
sections.text:
* '''Calendar month''' — Arial, all caps, expanded 1.2pt, left, exactly 15pt, after 8pt (size raised from 13pt; final value not recorded)
* '''Calendar year''' — based on month, right-aligned, recto only (select the last character → spacing Normal so the 0 doesn’t hang short)
* '''Calendar dayname''' — Arial 7 all caps, expanded 0.5pt, centred, exactly 10pt
* '''Calendar date''' — Arial 8, left, exactly 10pt, no leading zeros
* '''Calendar date muted''' — RGB 153/153/153 for spill days

sections.title: Rule hierarchy
sections.text:
# Month rule — 1½pt black, full page width
# Day-name bottom rule — ¾pt black, apply to Cell
# Grid — ½pt, RGB 102/102/102
# Notes lines — ½pt, RGB 191/191/191

sections.title: Build order
sections.text:
* '''Month line:''' a plain paragraph at the top of the page, NOT a text box. Confirm no empty paragraph above it.
* '''Full-page rule:''' Insert → Shapes → Line (hold Shift). Position: horizontal absolute 0″ right of Page; vertical absolute 0.58″ below Page. Untick “Move object with text”, THEN tick “Lock anchor”. In Front of Text. Width 7″, height 0″. Black, 1½pt.
* '''Table:''' insert 4 × 6; untick “Automatically resize to fit contents”; columns 1.47″; rows 1.38″ exactly; top-aligned; cell margins 0.04/0.05/0.05/0.04; borders ½pt RGB 102.
* '''Day-name row:''' Insert Above (inherits column widths — must be in the same table). Sun Tab Mon Tab Tue Tab Wed — no Tab after the last cell. 0.2″ exactly; T/B 0.02″, L/R 0.05″; bottom border ¾pt, apply to Cell.
* '''NOTES rules:''' split each cell individually into 1 × 4; all 24 sub-cells 0.34″ exactly, margins 0″, style Calendar date, interior horizontal borders ½pt RGB 191.

sections.title: Open items
sections.text:
* '''Clinical note typeface — unresolved.''' Courier New (dictated and transcribed) vs a clean sans (typed into an EHR). The year is 2030, so sans may be truer. Set the Reeves intake both ways and pick early — it’s the most-repeated register.
* '''Confirm the year is 2030.''' Every weekday in all twelve grids depends on it, and which day Eva’s standing appointment falls on.
* '''Month size.''' Raised from 13pt; final value not recorded. Check the 0.58″ rule and that six 1.38″ rows still fit.
* '''Print test, not yet done.''' Print the March verso at actual size, tape the spread at the fold, write a real week into it. The 1.16″ per cell is the whole gamble. If your hand needs more, the answer is an 8 × 10 trim — not taller rows (six at 1.5″ needs 9.0″ against 8.325″).
* '''Week-number column — optional, recommended.''' 0.22″ against the verso’s inside edge, Arial 6pt, 50% grey. A silent counter 1–52: when February shows weeks 49–52, the year is visibly running out.
* '''Notes line count.''' Four lines at 0.34″ assumes you write smaller in the notes column. If not, go to three.

sections.title: Corrections issued
sections.text:
Kept so they don’t get re-introduced:
* '''Verso margins:''' a verso is the LEFT page, so its spine is on the RIGHT. The month sits 0.375″ from the top and 0.375″ from the ''left'' (outer) edge.
* '''Hyphenation zone:''' the instruction to set 0.25″ was wrong; the field is disabled in .docx.
* '''Newsprint hed:''' unticking All caps was wrong — Newsprint has no All caps to inherit.
* '''Border merge fixes:''' alternating styles, 0.01″ offsets and 1-unit colour differences all fail.
* '''Month title in a text box:''' it was a paragraph border; the rule stopping short was correct behaviour; the actual cause was page parity.
